thread.title: GameStop Stock Is Falling Because the Sale of a Unit Isn't a Magic Bullet

title: GameStop Stock Is Falling Because the Sale of a Unit Isn't a Magic Bullet
text:
GameStop Stock Is Falling Because the Sale of a Unit Isn’t a Magic Bullet By Updated Nov. 23, 2018 3:58 p.m. ET Order Reprints Photograph by Patrick T. Fallon/Bloomberg Text size
GameStop (GME) stock is taking a hit after the company agreed to sell its Spring Mobile division .
Where we were: On Wednesday afternoon, GameStop stock was halted ahead of its announcement of the sale.
Where we’re headed: The divestiture may be a step in the right direction, but not enough for analysts to get more bullish on the struggling stock.
With the stock down more than 26%, it hasn’t been much fun being a GameStop investor this year.
The company is dealing with the same issues facing retail as a whole, including shifting consumer habits and e-commerce competition, but on top of that GameStop is dealing with the fact that many gamers are opting for digital downloads, as well as the slower pace of content from game makers.
Earlier this week, GameStop said it agreed to sell its Spring Mobile division to Prime Communications L.P. for $700 million in a transaction expected to close before the end of the year. Spring Mobile operates nearly 1,300 AT&T (T) wireless stores.
Analysts are weighing in on the move Friday. Loop Capital’s Anthony Chukumba writes that it’s a step in the right direction, as the unit has been “a growing albatross for GameStop over the past few years, driven by a combination of slowing smartphone sales as consumers hold onto their devices longer and AT&T’s restructuring of Spring Mobile’s economics in an attempt to drive more DirecTV subscriptions.”
He’s glad that the sale will allow management to refocus on the core videogame business, but writes that this shouldn’t prevent GameStop from being bought as a whole. “In fact, we think a “pure-play” GameStop will be even more attractive to financial sponsors, who will no longer have to worry about divesting the business themselves.” Chukumba reiterated a Hold rating and $16 price target on the stock.
Telsey Advisory Group’s Joseph Feldman also has a Market Perform rating, and $14 price target on GameStop. He writes that the Spring Mobile sale should be welcome news, and the “ongoing strategic review provides some support for the stock.” Nonetheless, he’s still on the sidelines, as he believes that profits from the sale of accessories, collectibles, and digital streams might not be enough to “fill the anticipated gap from the structural pressures on the physical videogame business over the next few years.”
Feldman also notes that this is an about-face for GameStop, which originally bought Spring Mobile to diversify its sales base away from just gaming. He estimates that between 2013 and 2016, the company spent as much as $750 million to buy AT&T and Apple (AAPL) resellers. So while the divestiture is “a clear indication that GameStop is focused on reviving its gaming business and growing collectibles,” the $700 million price tag shows that the company may not recoup all that it spent.
GameStop is down 2.5% to $13.37 in recent trading.
